findings.title: endianness argument accepts any string with no validation, silently producing wrong bytes
findings.description: __init__ types endianness as Literal["big", "little", "source_else_big"] but never validates it at runtime. Any string is stored verbatim. Because __bytes__ tests `if self.endianness == "big": ... else: reverse`, a common typo/variant like "Little", "LE", or "BE" is silently treated as little-endian and yields byte-reversed output with no error — a silent-wrong trap that only surfaces as corrupted binary far downstream. str()/repr() also happily print the bogus tag (UInt8[LE]), reinforcing the false sense that it was accepted correctly.
findings.evidence:
UInt8(1, endianness='LE') succeeds; `u.endianness == 'LE'`; str(u) == 'UInt8[LE](1 = 00000001)'. __bytes__: "if self.endianness == 'big':
            return temp_bytes
        else:
            return temp_bytes[::-1]" — so 'LE'/'Little'/'BE' all fall into the little-endian (reverse) branch.
findings.suggestion: After resolving source_else_big, validate: `if endianness not in ('big', 'little'): raise ValueError(f"endianness must be 'big' or 'little', got {endianness!r}")`. Fail fast at construction rather than mis-serializing later.
findings.verifyReason: Verified against current code and confirmed empirically. In bytemaker/bittypes/bittype.py, __init__ (lines 117-151) types endianness as Literal["big","little","source_else_big"] but never validates it at runtime; after resolving "source_else_big" it just does `self._endianness = endianness`, storing any string verbatim. __bytes__ (lines 332-336) tests `if self.endianness == "big": return temp_bytes else: return temp_bytes[::-1]`, so ANY non-"big" string falls into the reverse (little-endian) branch. I reproduced it: UInt8(1, endianness='LE') constructs fine, u.endianness == 'LE', str(u) == 'UInt8[LE](1 = 00000001)'; and the multi-byte case proves the silent-wrong trap — UInt16(258, endianness='BE') yields b'\x02\x01', byte-reversed from the intended big-endian b'\x01\x02', with no error. A user typing 'BE' meaning big-endian silently gets little-endian bytes that only surface as corrupted binary far downstream. This is a genuine ux/foot-gun, not a nitpick and not the intentional narrative-docstring style. It is strengthened by an in-repo inconsistency: the new headline Struct system already validates this exact contract (structs.py:754-755: `if endian not in ("big","little"): raise PlanCompileError(f"{name}: endian must be 'big' or 'little'")`), so the legacy BitType path is the odd one out, and the suggested fix mirrors an already-established pattern. Severity kept at medium rather than high: the mis-serialization only triggers when a caller supplies a non-canonical string, and the Literal type hint plus a type-checker steer correct usage away from the trap — it does not bite correct/typed callers. Confidence high (behavior proven by execution and source). Minor note: the finding's aside that str()/repr() "reinforce the false sense" is accurate but secondary; the load-bearing silent-wrong-bytes claim is fully solid. Not a July regression (same logic exists in the ~4-week-old reference pyc), but the ux lens is about present behavior, and it is present.

findings.title: Typo'd endianness (e.g. 'bigg', 'litle') is silently accepted through the Int/SInt/UInt constructors and treated as little-endian
findings.description: The SInt/UInt constructors (and the base __init__ they forward to) declare endianness as a Literal['big','little','source_else_big'] but never validate the string. Because the byte-order logic only special-cases exactly 'big' (else it reverses), any typo silently produces LITTLE-endian output. UInt16(0x0102, endianness='bigg') yields bytes 0201 — the opposite of what the user intended — with no error or warning. A wrong byte order is exactly the kind of silent-wrong bug this library exists to prevent, and it stems from a one-character typo being accepted. (Root cause is the base BitType.__init__/__bytes__ in bittype.py, but it manifests directly through the int.py constructors, which re-declare and forward endianness without validation.)
findings.evidence:
def __init__(self, ..., endianness: Literal["big", "little", "source_else_big"] = "source_else_big", ...):
    ...
    super().__init__(source=source, value=value, bits=bits, endianness=endianness)

# observed:
#   bytes(UInt16(0x0102, endianness='big'))   -> 0102
#   bytes(UInt16(0x0102, endianness='bigg'))  -> 0201  (silently little-endian)
#   bytes(UInt16(0x0102, endianness='litle')) -> 0201  (silently little-endian)
findings.suggestion: Validate endianness against {'big','little','source_else_big'} in __init__ (ideally in the base BitType.__init__) and raise ValueError naming the bad value and the valid options, so a typo fails loudly at construction instead of silently flipping byte order.
findings.verifyReason: Verified in current code and empirically reproduced. In bittype.py, BitType.__init__ (lines 148-151) stores the endianness string unvalidated: if it isn't "source_else_big" it is assigned to self._endianness as-is. __bytes__ (lines 333-336) then special-cases only "big" (`if self.endianness == "big": return temp_bytes else: return temp_bytes[::-1]`), so any other string — including a typo — falls into the else branch and yields reversed (little-endian) bytes. I ran it: bytes(UInt16(0x0102, endianness='big')) -> 0102, but endianness='bigg' and endianness='litle' both -> 0201, the opposite byte order, with no error or warning. The SInt/UInt __init__ in int.py (lines 571-587) re-declare endianness as Literal["big","little","source_else_big"] and forward it to super().__init__ without validation, so the false-precision type hint manifests directly through the int.py constructors as the report states; the citation and root-cause attribution are accurate. grep confirms no ValueError/assert/validation on endianness anywhere in bittype.py. This is a genuine silent-wrong bug (wrong byte order from a one-character typo) — exactly the failure class this C-analogous serialization library exists to prevent — not a nitpick and not a complaint about the intentional narrative docstring style. Raising confidence to high given the empirical reproduction; keeping severity at medium since it requires user typo to trigger and does not affect correct-input paths (below the "actively misleading / breakage on normal use" high bar). Note for prioritization: the source_else_big string appears in the REF tree's compiled bittype.pyc, so this validation gap predates the July rewrite rather than being a new regression, but it is currently present and worth a loud ValueError at construction.

findings.title: Typo'd endianness value is silently treated as big-endian instead of rejected
findings.description: endianness is typed Literal['big','little'] but never validated at runtime. The code only special-cases the exact string 'little' (reverses); any other value, including a typo like 'litle' or 'small', falls through to the big-endian path and produces wrong bytes with no error. The same all-branches-else-is-big pattern appears in to_bytes_aggregate/ctype_to_bytes (endianness != sys.byteorder / == 'little'). This is a classic silent-wrong footgun that surfaces only as corrupted output far downstream.
findings.evidence: pytype_to_bytes: if endianness == "little": retval = retval[::-1]. Verified: pytype_to_bytes(1, endianness='litle') == b'\x00\x00\x00\x01' (silently big-endian, no error), identical to endianness='big'.
findings.suggestion: Validate at entry: if endianness not in ('big','little'): raise ValueError(f"endianness must be 'big' or 'little', got {endianness!r}"). Apply consistently across pytypes/ctypes_/aggregate_types entry points.
findings.verifyReason: Verified in current code and reproduced at runtime. In bytemaker/conversions/pytypes.py, pytype_to_bytes (lines 281-299) and bytes_to_pytype (lines 324-343) only special-case the exact string "little" (`if endianness == "little": retval = retval[::-1]`); every other value falls through to big-endian. Ran it: pytype_to_bytes(1, endianness='litle') == b'\x00\x00\x00\x01', byte-identical to endianness='big', no error; same for 'small'. The Literal["big","little"] type hint is not enforced at runtime, so a mistyped literal silently yields wrong bytes downstream. The "same pattern elsewhere" claim also checks out: ctypes_.py:96,149 use `endianness != sys.byteorder` and aggregate_types.py:171 uses `"<" if endianness == "little" else ">"`, so a typo silently corrupts output in every conversion entry point. One nuance the report glosses: on the ctypes path a typo takes the reverse-of-host branch rather than a literal big-endian path, so the direction of the wrongness is actually inconsistent across paths — which strengthens the case rather than weakening it. This is a genuine silent-wrong footgun, not a nitpick and not the intentional narrative-docstring style; the suggested entry-point ValueError validation is concrete and actionable. Medium (not high) is fair because these are internal conversion helpers reachable only via a caller-side string error, not the headline Struct API. Confidence high: behavior directly reproduced.
